name: The African Butter Tree of the Healing Garden

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, Healing Garden (behind Block 5)

access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15-20 minute walk to the Healing Garden
story:
The seeds of this tree are roughly forty percent fat, and West Africa presses them for butter. That is what brought it to Singapore. In 1897 the Botanic Gardens had it sent from Sierra Leone and planted in the Economic Garden, the plot where the colony tested which tropical crops could be made to pay. Pentadesma butyracea grows wild from Guinea to Cameroon and nowhere in Southeast Asia. The oil never became a business here, and the experiment settled into being a specimen instead.

NParks calls this tree likely a remnant of that original introduction and says it has stood on this spot for more than a century. That word likely is why its age sits as a band, roughly 110 to 140 years, rather than a date. The measurements are firmer: 3.2 metres round in 2003, 3.6 metres now, and 18 metres of crown over the Healing Garden.

A survey of Southeast Asian plant resources records the species growing successfully in Singapore by about 1900, which confirms the experiment took even though the trade never did.

The fruit is the size of a fist, ten to twelve centimetres, with a rind that takes a knife and a yellow greasy juice inside. The seeds within are the part anyone wanted. It now stands in the Healing Garden behind Block 5, doing nothing commercial at all.

name: The Teak of the Botany Centre

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, along Office Ring Road, Botany Centre

access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 10-15 minute walk to the Botany Centre
story:
Teak needs a dry season, and Singapore has never had one. NParks says so on this tree's own record: the species struggles in a climate without an annual drought. This one dates from 1884 by NParks' own dating, which puts it at about 140 years, and it has spent all of them growing in conditions its species is not built for. Girth 2.9 metres, height 20.6 metres.

Tectona grandis belongs to the monsoon forests of Myanmar, Thailand, India and Indochina, where it drops its leaves through the dry months. Singapore does not supply them. The tree stands instead along Office Ring Road beside the Botany Centre, which is about as far from a monsoon forest as a teak is likely to get.

Its timber is the reason anyone knows the word. Teak is loaded with natural oils that see off termites and shrug off water, which is why it has decked ships for centuries and why teak furniture tends to outlive the people who buy it. Plantations across the tropics exist for that one property.

This one was never cut. It has stood since 1884 and the only thing anybody has ever taken from it is a measurement. For a species valued almost entirely by the cubic metre, that counts as an unusual career.

name: The Nemesu of the Rainforest

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, Rainforest, visible from Lower Ring Road (near the Heritage Mengkulang)

access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee. The tree itself stands inside the six-hectare rainforest patch and is not approached directly, but NParks' own page says it 'can be viewed from a nearby footpath' and it is 'easily viewed from Lower Ring Road'.
transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15 minute walk to the rainforest section
story:
Forty-four and a half metres is roughly a fourteen-storey building, and that is the height of this tree, standing in the middle of Singapore. The nemesu is an emergent dipterocarp, built to push a straight bole clear of everything around it, and the species can carry that trunk to sixty metres. This one is six metres round at chest height, thick even by the standards of the city's heritage register.

It is also an endangered species, and this tree did not arrive in a pot. It stands inside the six hectares of surviving rainforest held within the Singapore Botanic Gardens, ground the Gardens grew around rather than laid out. UNESCO listed the Gardens as a World Heritage Site in 2015.

You do not walk up to it. NParks says it can be seen from a nearby footpath and is easily viewed from Lower Ring Road. The rainforest patch is not somewhere to wander into, and the tree is big enough that this hardly matters. Look for scaly bark and the plank buttresses spreading from its base.

The species has a road named after it across town, Nemesu Avenue by Lower Peirce Reservoir. Nobody has published this tree's age, and dipterocarp growth varies too much from site to site to work one out from the girth. If anyone has a figure, we would like it.

name: The Mengkulang of the Gardens' Jungle

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, along Lower Ring Road, near the Bandstand

access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15 minute walk to the rainforest section near the Bandstand
story:
In 1908 Henry Ridley described a species new to science, and the material came off this tree. Heritiera elata is pinned to it: that is what a type specimen is, the individual the name itself refers back to. Ridley was the Botanic Gardens' first Director, and his note on these trees reads like a man who already had a favourite. There are two or three of these fine trees in the Gardens' Jungle, he wrote. The finest is a conspicuous object by the plant sheds.

The Gardens' Jungle is still there, a patch of remnant rainforest held inside the Botanic Gardens, and it has produced a run of type specimens over the years. A 2022 paper from the National University of Singapore, cataloguing the plants first described from Singapore ground, lists this species among them.

The trunk is the giveaway. Its plank buttresses fold vertically, in pleats running up from the base, a feature unique to the species. Four and a half metres round, twenty-six metres tall, standing along Lower Ring Road near the Bandstand.

Its age is genuinely unknown. NParks says it is probably older than the Gardens, which were laid out in 1859, but that is an impression rather than a measurement, and nobody has put a number on it. If you know better, tell us.
